newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives see jobs data election boost.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives see jobs data election boost.

text.p: Britain's Conservatives, fighting to get back on terms with the Labour opposition ahead of an imminent election, on Wednesday greeted a hefty fall in unemployment as evidence that their economic policies were working.

Two senior ministers called a news conference to trumpet the announcement of a 67,800 drop in jobless benefit claimants in January and to say Labour would reverse the downward trend by importing job-destroying workplace rules from Europe.

Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang said British unemployment was now down to 1.8 million, or 6.5 percent of the workforce, but the jobless rate in other major European Union countries ranged from 11.3 percent in Germany to 14.2 percent in Spain.
"Labour risks putting 1.5 million people out of work by dragging Britain into the European social model," he said.
"If we had the same percentage jobless rate as the major continental economies, unemployment would leap to 3.5 million."
Labour has vowed to introduce the EU's Social Chapter on workers' rights if it wins an election, due by May 22.

Education and Employment Secretary Gillian Shephard said the drop in unemployment to the lowest rate for six years was a reward for changes made to the way Britain's labour market operates since the Conservatives came to power in 1979.
"Old restrictions have been abolished and proposals for new burdens such as the Social Chapter or a national minimum wage resisted," she said.
Labour has also pledged to introduce a minimum wage but has not yet fixed the level.
The Conservatives say Labour's plans are bound to increase the cost of employing British workers and to deter many firms from increasing employment.

Labour employment spokesman David Blunkett said 137,000 people had disappeared from the official figures since October, not because they had found jobs but because of the introduction of a jobseekers allowance to replace unemployment benefit.

He said the official figures hid unemployment blackspots in many British cities and added that only Labour's plan to use a windfall tax on the profits of privatised companies to help 250,000 young people into work could help these areas.
"The Conservatives offer no hope to people in areas of high long-term unemployment," Blunkett said.

British newspapers on Wednesday said that Prime Minister John Major must decide this week whether to call an early election on March 20 or to soldier on until May 1, which he has indicated is his preferred date.
Conservative Party chairman Brian Mawhinney, asked whether the jobless data provided an ideal launchpad for an early election, gave no clue as to Major's thinking on timing.
"Whenever the Prime Minister announces a date, we will be ready for the election," he replied.
Recent opinion polls have been slightly more encouraging for the Conservatives but still put them almost 20 percentage points behind the Labour Party of moderate Tony Blair.
